name: Diego Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Diego, thanks for this. I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI firms, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will have your name on it. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the site crew for a modular housing firm, so our houses get built as big boxes in a factory forty miles away, then come in on lorries and get craned onto the foundations. On the Meadow Lane estate we're doing sixty homes. My job is guiding the boxes down, bolting them together, fixing the roof joins and doing the finishing carpentry where the boxes meet, the skirting and trims that hide the joints. Hannah, the site supervisor, runs the crane plan off a tablet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's fast, a house goes from empty plot to roof on in a day, which still feels like magic. The hard part is the finishing, because the boxes are never quite level and I'm still not good at hiding a bad join. I use AI every day, I take photos of a gap and ask it how a proper joiner would trim it. Kofi, who's been doing this ten years, laughs at me, then asks to see the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but still handy, and I'd keep using it. Online I'd post something like, the tools are good, the hype was silly. At work nobody would really notice the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's in good shape either way. Modular building is growing, there are three firms like ours within an hour, and I'm paid well because I'll go anywhere. The only thing I'd think is that I need to get better at finishing, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the crew, keep using AI to learn the finishing tricks, and keep my weekend thing going. I buy old furniture at house clearances, fix it up in my lock-up and sell it online, which makes me about four hundred a month. I've got the van paid off and about eight months of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the furniture side.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It started with a broken oak dresser I found on the street outside a house clearance. I watched videos, asked the AI how to fix the drawer runners, and sold it for two hundred. Now I do about three pieces a month. The AI writes the furniture listings, I do the sanding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'd still be slow at the finishing, which is my own problem. And maybe that Kofi's knees are going and he's not sure how long he can keep climbing on the boxes. That's nothing to do with AI though.

say: I'd call AI **overhyped but handy**, and keep using it.
Online I'd say the **tools are good** and the hype was silly.
think: Modular building is **growing**, with **three firms** like ours within an hour.
I still need to get better at **finishing**, AI or not.
do: Keep using AI to learn **finishing tricks** at the box joints.
Keep the weekend **furniture business** making about four hundred a month.
Hold onto **eight months** of savings and the paid-off van.
S0.quote: The AI writes the furniture listings, I do the sanding.
fieldNote: He already works for the **disruptor**: factory-built homes craned onto site.
His **side business** is real money and already uses AI for **listings**.
His only worry here is **skill**, plus a colleague's knees.

steps.text: Keep using AI photos to learn how to trim box joints
Keep fixing and selling three furniture pieces a month
Carry on with the Meadow Lane modular crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, get on with it. Learn the tools, change how you work, and stop moaning. That's what I'd say to the crew, though I'd say it a bit nicer to Kofi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. Our firm already moved most of the building into a factory, and AI planning just makes the crane days smoother. The office jobs at the firm might shrink, the people booking lorries and ordering parts, but on site we still need hands for a few years yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI planning tools Hannah uses, so I can be the one who runs crane days when she's off. I'd grow the furniture side, maybe buy a better sander and a spray booth for about two thousand. And I'd ask the firm if I could spend a week in the factory to see how the robot arms work there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the week in the factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the factory already has robot arms that nail the wall frames, and that's where things are heading. If I understand how they work, I'm useful on both ends. Hannah says nobody from site has ever asked, which is exactly why I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office jobs might shrink. Who would you think of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman called Jo who books every lorry and every crane slot. She's brilliant but she does it all on the phone and a spreadsheet. I'd worry about her, honestly. If she asked, I'd show her the AI tools, but some people don't want to be shown.

say: It's here, so **learn the tools** and change how you work.
I'd tell the crew to **stop moaning**, but say it nicer to Kofi.
think: AI planning makes **crane days** smoother, so it's good for me.
**Office jobs** like lorry booking might shrink, but site work needs **hands** for years.
do: Learn the **AI planning tools** to run crane days when Hannah's off.
Spend about **two thousand** on a sander and spray booth for furniture.
Ask for a **week in the factory** to see the robot arms.
S1.quote: The factory already has robot arms that nail the wall frames, and that's where things are heading.
fieldNote: He sees himself on the **winning side** of the change, which fits his adaptive style.
He wants to understand **robots early**, by visiting the factory.
His concern for **Jo**, the lorry booker, shows he sees who loses.

steps.text: Learn the AI crane planning tools the supervisor uses
Buy a two-thousand sander and spray booth for furniture
Ask for a week in the factory to learn the robot arms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is massive and people need to stop pretending it isn't. I'd tell my mates to save money and learn the tools now, not later. Online I'd be the one sharing practical stuff, courses, grants, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scary even for me. AI does Hannah's planning and Jo's booking in 2028, and by 2031 the robots can do what I do, the guiding, the bolting and the finishing. Modular is the easiest building for robots, because everything's made to measure in a factory. I'd be thirty-one and I'd need to already be somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get onto any course the firm or the factory runs on operating and fixing the robots, even unpaid. I'd move savings into cash and cut the furniture spending. And I'd use AI to run the furniture side fully, listings, prices and customer messages, so it's a real second income if the site goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but this is a lot of change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the window. In 2028 I'd see the planners and bookers go, and I'd know the site crew is next. Three years is long enough to become the guy who looks after the robots on site, if I start the day the AI news hits. If I wait until 2030, I'm too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the furniture business be enough to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as it is, four hundred a month is pocket money. If I pushed it with AI doing the selling, maybe a thousand. Plus savings, that's a year or two of bridge. Robots might do furniture too eventually, but people like old pieces with a story, and that's me telling it.

say: This is **massive**, and people need to stop **pretending** otherwise.
I'd tell mates to **save money** and learn the tools now, and share courses online.
think: Modular homes are the **easiest building** for robots, since factory parts fit exactly.
By **2031** I'd be thirty-one and need to already be **somewhere else**.
do: Take any course on **operating and fixing** robots, even unpaid.
Move savings into **cash** and cut furniture spending.
Use AI to run the **furniture business** fully as a second income.
S2.quote: Modular is the easiest building for robots, because everything's made to measure in a factory.
fieldNote: He knows his niche, **modular**, is especially **robot-friendly**.
He treats the **three-year gap** as a window that closes if he waits.
The **furniture business** becomes a planned bridge, not a hobby.

steps.text: Join any robot operating and repair course, even unpaid
Move savings into cash and cut furniture spending
Let AI run listings and messages for the furniture business
Grow the furniture side to about a thousand a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's five years, so use them. Learn, save and get close to the machines. I'd keep sharing courses online like I said for the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots on site around 2034 means I'm thirty-five and I've had a good run on the crew. I'd plan to move to the factory side well before then, maybe in 2030. It's still fast, but I think I can be ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to work in the factory for a year or two, learning the robot arms, then come back to site as the robot lead when they arrive. I'd keep the furniture going and use part of my savings to buy a second-hand electric van for it. I'd use the AI planning tools every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More curious than scared, but uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't moving to the factory a pay cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, the site pay's better because of the travelling. But a year of lower pay to be one of the few people who knows the robots seems like a good trade. I've got the savings to cover it. Kofi says I'm mad, then says he'd do the same if he was my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would worry, she always does. My dad ran a kebab shop for twenty years and always said you have to change the menu before the customers get bored. I'd tell them I'm changing the menu early.

say: There's **five years**, so use them to learn, save and get close to the **machines**.
I'd keep **sharing courses** online for anyone who wants them.
think: Robots on site around **2034** means I'm thirty-five after a good run.
Moving to the **factory side** by about 2030 keeps me **ahead** of it.
do: Apply to work in the **factory** for a year or two learning robot arms.
Buy a **second-hand electric van** for the furniture business.
Use the **AI planning tools** every day.
S3.quote: My dad ran a kebab shop for twenty years and always said you have to change the menu before the customers get bored.
fieldNote: He would take a **pay cut** in the factory to learn robots before they reach site.
His dad's **kebab shop** gives him a simple rule for change.
Five years turns his plan from a scramble into a **deliberate move**.

steps.text: Move to the factory for a year to learn the robot arms
Buy a second-hand electric van for the furniture business
Use the AI crane planning tools every working day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads, so there's no reason for anyone to be caught out. Firms should train people and people should take the training. That's the deal I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with robots around 2039 I'd be forty, probably running a site crew by then. The thinking parts of that, the planning and the paperwork, go to AI in 2036, but that frees me up for the people and the machines. I think I'd do well out of this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the crew and aim for supervisor in a few years. Keep growing the furniture side and maybe rent a small workshop. I'd put some savings into shares in the firms making building robots, so I win a bit either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, it sounds like a good decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy shares in robot makers. Isn't that betting against your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying shares in the robot makers is more like insurance: if the robots take site work, the shares go up and that softens it. If they don't, I've still got the job. I wouldn't put more than a few thousand in though, I'm not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the workshop for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More furniture, maybe some custom pieces, built-in shelves for people's homes. That's carpentry I'm slowly getting better at. By the time robots can do house building, I'd want a little business that sells things people want made by a person.

say: **Ten years** is loads, so nobody should be **caught out**.
Firms should **train** people, and people should **take the training**.
think: By **2039** I'd be forty and probably running a **site crew**.
AI takes the **paperwork** in 2036, freeing me for people and machines.
do: Aim for **site supervisor** in a few years.
Rent a **small workshop** and grow the furniture side.
Put a few thousand into **shares** in building robot makers.
S4.quote: Buying shares in the robot makers is more like insurance: if the robots take site work, the shares go up and that softens it.
fieldNote: With a decade, he expects to **gain**, aiming for supervisor and a workshop.
He **hedges** his job risk with shares in robot makers.
He sees **hand-made** pieces as a long-term niche.

steps.text: Work towards site supervisor on the modular crew
Rent a small workshop for furniture and custom shelves
Put a few thousand into shares of robot makers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Modular is the first place the robots will land, and three years isn't long. What would help is the firms running proper paid training on their robots for the site crews, before they arrive, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who I'd trust about all this. Not the news, not the tech firms. Kofi, my mate on the crew, because he's seen every new gadget come through in ten years and he tells it straight.

headlineQuote: Modular is the first place the robots will land, and three years isn't long.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old site carpenter** on a modular housing crew, still learning the finishing.
He owns his van, has **eight months saved** and runs a weekend furniture business.
He uses **AI every day** and moves early, planning a factory stint to learn the robots.
Pragmatic, he blames nobody and expects people and firms to **train**.
He stays **calm** in most pictures, becoming **anxious** only when robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because modular sites are where robots land **first**.
whatWouldHelp: Firms running **paid training** on their robots for site crews **before** they arrive.
